Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Catalina Reyes was changing in the dim hallway of the community center when the man lunged. A heavy glass bottle struck the plaster wall, and he swept a long wooden chair leg across the floor like a weapon. She remembers the sharp glint of metal and the blur of wood, the sudden violence knocking her against the cool tiles. She had been halfway out of her dress, the fabric pooled at her ankles, and the exposure of her bare skin to the draft made her feel entirely unprotected. Even now, the visual of those objects—the bottle, the chair leg, the umbrella he later raised—remains locked in her mind as concrete threats. She knows exactly what happened in that hallway, yet she cannot find words to describe it when her husband asks. The memories do not arrive in a straight line; she recalls the sound of the glass before the sight of the man’s face, the heat of the violence before the chill of the bare floor. When the sequence surfaces, a sharp, sudden rage rises in her chest. In the months that followed, Catalina’s body settled into a state of quiet alertness. She found herself jumpy, her shoulders tightening at the sudden slam of a car door or the unexpected clatter of dishes. Even when her husband placed a hand on her arm and told her the house was secure, she found it impossible to believe it. Safety felt like a temporary arrangement rather than a settled fact. This unease deepened as the weeks passed, but it was the nights that grew hardest to endure. She found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, the darkness magnifying every creak of the floorboards into a potential breach. She began avoiding the hallway mirror, the sight of her own bare shoulders in the glass pulling the assault back into the present. Her routine at the non-profit office adapted around these shifts; she started arriving early and leaving after the rest of the staff had gone, preferring the quiet hum of the workstations to the unpredictable comings and goings of the day. The assault lingered in how Catalina viewed herself and her place in the world. She had come to believe she was a weak person, her body a site of fragility rather than strength. During staff meetings, she watched her colleagues navigate crises with apparent ease and was certain that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. Her attendance at Sunday gatherings and neighborhood festivals dwindled, and she felt the slow unraveling of her connection to her community and culture. The familiar cadence of Spanish conversations and the warmth of shared meals now felt like demands she could no longer meet. At the office, her job as a non-profit worker required constant coordination with local families, and she noticed how her hesitation to leave the building during evening outreach visits marked a quiet gap in her professional responsibilities. Her husband adjusted his routine to meet her, but the distance between them was not one of disagreement, simply of different rhythms. Now, at thirty-nine, Catalina sits in the intake room with a notebook resting in her lap. She has come to realize that the quiet routine she built is no longer enough to contain the jumpy tension or the stubborn unbelief that the night will hold. She is here; the inability to trust safety has begun to color her days, and the rage on recall no longer fades as quickly as it once did. What she hopes for is not a complete erasure of the memory, but a steadier ground beneath her feet. She is most afraid of returning to the state of exposure, of feeling again the sudden violence and the weight of those visual threats, but she is ready to step outside the quiet bubble she has made, to let the words come even if they do not arrive in the right order, and to find her way back to the people she has loved.
